The words

He who would valiant be 'gainst all disaster,
Let him in constancy follow the Master.
There's no discouragement shall make him once relent
His first avowed intent to be a pilgrim.

Who so beset him round with dismal stories
Do but themselves confound his strength the more is.
No foes shall stay his might; though he with giants fight,
He will make good his right to be a pilgrim.

Since, Lord, Thou dost defend us with Thy Spirit,
We know we at the end, shall life inherit.
Then fancies flee away! I'll fear not what men say,
I'll labor night and day to be a pilgrim.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (D), on the word “He”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

The words are by John Bunyan and Percy Dearmer, first published in 1684. The tune, MONKS GATE, is Traditional English. This version of the melody and the words comes from the Open Hymnal Project.

  • Words (1684): John Bunyan (1628–1688)
  • Words (1684): Percy Dearmer (1867–1936)
  • Melody: Traditional English

Questions about He Who Would Valiant Be

What is the doh of He Who Would Valiant Be?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does He Who Would Valiant Be start on?

It starts on d (D in D major), a pickup on the word “He” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is He Who Would Valiant Be in the public domain?

Yes. John Bunyan died in 1688, Percy Dearmer died in 1936; the words were first published in 1684 and the music in 1904. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in Nigeria, the UK, the EU and the United States. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
